# Button Mash, full context

# Button Mash

The universal in-browser game console. Three centerpieces: (1) the Player: a bring-your-own-file EmulatorJS console for 20+ classic systems (the site hosts zero ROMs; the user's file never leaves their machine); (2) the Converter 3.0, batch-convert GBA, GB/GBC, NES, SNES or Genesis files you own into self-contained playable .html browser games (client-side only, all five cores BIOS-free, honest validation, compression levels); (3) the Party Planner, headcount + time + vibe in, timed game-night rotation plan out. Plus a curated directory of 213 free, legal browser games (every link verified live 2026-10-11), hand-built collections, genre deep dives, and legal-lane emulation guides. No ROM piracy links, no cracked-game sites, no commercial ROM downloads, ever.

## Play
- player.html, the bring-your-own-file Player (EmulatorJS, 20+ systems, save states, fullscreen; Player 2.1: named save slots + auto-save, per-system keyboard+gamepad remap, cheat-code entry, display options (CRT/integer-scale/aspect, per-system quick settings), honest netplay notes)
- converter.html: Converter 3.0: batch ROM-to-browser-game conversion (GBA/GB/GBC/NES/SNES/Genesis files in, one self-contained .html per file out), 5 BIOS-free cores (mGBA/Gambatte/FCEUmm/Snes9x/Genesis Plus GX), 4 compression levels + presets, honest ROM validation (refuses empty/all-zero/bad-NES, warns on blank headers / missing SEGA string, keeps SNES copier headers), custom titles + cover art, ▶ Player mode deep links
- party-planner.html: Party planner 2.0: guest list (2-16 names), per-guest game voting (ties go to the earliest-picked game), fair rotation scheduler (hot-seat groups of 4), party timeline with snack break + tournament slot, snack-break timer, kids-party mode from the 75 kid-safe games, tournament handoff 2.0 (?players=N&names=A,B&games=ids&format=), shareable #p= party links, print party pack + copy-as-text
- game-night.html: Game Night: the Curator deals your night, headcount (1-12) + time (15-240 min) + vibe + skill mix + kids flag in, marquee lineup out (warm-up, main events, showdown/deep-dive, cool-down) with per-game session + skill-floor curator estimates, genre variety, timebox fit, and a staggered marquee ceremony reveal; client-side from the 213-game verified catalog, nothing sent; dealt nights can be saved in the browser (bm.lineups.v1) and rematched with fresh picks on the same setup
- tournament.html: Tournament 2.0: single- or double-elimination brackets for game night (2-16 players, manual seeding UI + randomize, honest byes, best-of-N per round, per-round game voting from the full catalog, match history + undo, shareable bracket links, localStorage saves, print + copy-my-bracket; accepts the party planner handoff (?players=N&games=ids))
- tournament-night.html: Tournament Night: a bracket night for the games themselves, pick a saved Game Night lineup or a collection, seed its real games in source order on the bracket engine, pick winners round by round (picks persist in bm.tournament-night.v1), crown a champion, copy the plain-text results card
- versus.html?a=<id>&b=<id>: Versus: any two catalog games side by side from their real records (year named in the description, collections, genre, controls, tags, Kids corner pass, written coverage); the verdict strip reports only what the data supports (older/newer, shelf footprint, coverage, Kids pass), no scores, no winner; thin record pairs get an honest no-basis state; share card + pairing link
- games.html, the 213-game directory (search incl. tags, genre + tag filters, shareable URL views, favorites, random game, game of the day)
- game.html?id=<game-id>, per-game metadata file: description, controls, kid-safe + multiplayer + vibe marks (live Curator enrichment with honest live/cached badge), curated-shelf cross-links, played/beaten tracking, shareable game-file links, prev/next through the catalog
- trophy-room.html: The Trophy Room: persistent play-tracking (mark games played/beaten on any game card; per-genre completion dials, 16-prize achievement case, per-collection progress; JSON export/import with schema validation; all browser-local)
- kids.html: Kids corner: 113 kid-safe games (no chat, no unmoderated multiplayer, no gambling, no graphic/horror content), age bands 5-7 / 8-10 / 11-12, parent notes, reduced-motion default
- parents.html, parent guide: curation method, honesty policy (assessments not guarantees, play the first 10 minutes together), common-sense screen-time tips, save-state 'one more level' trick
- collections.html, 24 hand-built collections
- genres/roguelike.html, genres/cozy.html, genres/puzzle.html, genres/retro.html, genres/action.html, genres/multiplayer.html, genres/idle.html, genres/horror.html, genre deep dives with start-here picks (all eight genres, the set is complete)
- journal.html: Play journal & backlog (T-MASH-2): per-game status shelves (want to play / playing / finished) and dated log entries, multiple per playthrough, for all 213 catalog games; persisted in this browser only (localStorage bm.journal.v1), no account, no server

- SameBoy [GB, GBC], Cycle-accurate Game Boy / Color emulation, beautifully maintained. https://sameboy.github.io/
- Mesen [NES, SNES, GB, GBC], The most accurate NES emulator ever made, with a legendary debugger. Also covers SNES/GB. https://mesen.ca/
- DuckStation [PlayStation] (needs your own dumped BIOS), Modern, fast PlayStation emulator with gorgeous upscaling. Relicensed Sept 2024: GPL-3.0 until then, now source-available under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (not open source). https://www.duckstation.org/
- PCSX2 [PlayStation 2] (needs your own dumped BIOS), The long-reigning PS2 emulator, still actively improved. https://pcsx2.net/
- PPSSPP [PSP], Plays the PSP library at HD resolutions on almost anything. https://www.ppsspp.org/
- Dolphin [GameCube, Wii], GameCube and Wii emulation at HD resolutions. One of the most polished emulators ever made. https://dolphin-emu.org/
- webretro [Many via libretro cores], RetroArch cores in the browser via a clean web frontend. Good alternative embedding option. https://github.com/BinBashBanana/webretro

# Guides (full text)

## EmulatorJS self-hosting guide
Difficulty: Intermediate · ~30 min · slug: emulatorjs-self-hosting

Host the open-source EmulatorJS player on your own site and play ROMs you dumped yourself, setup, cores, BIOS, and the legal line.

### What it is (and the legal line)

EmulatorJS is a free, open-source project that puts classic console emulation in a web page. It bundles libretro cores compiled to WebAssembly, so systems from the NES to the GBA run right in the browser with no plugins.

The software itself is completely legal, and it ships with zero games. You supply the game files, and this is the part that matters: only load ROMs you dumped from cartridges or discs you own, plus homebrew and public-domain titles. Downloading commercial ROMs you don't own is piracy, no matter how nicely the player is skinned.

### What you need

- A web host that serves static files (any static host works), or just your own computer for local play
- ROM files you dumped yourself, see the rip-your-own-cartridges guide
- For some systems, a BIOS file dumped from hardware you own (GBA and PlayStation cores need one)
- About 30 minutes

### 1. Get the release

Grab the latest release ZIP from the project's GitHub releases page (github.com/EmulatorJS/EmulatorJS) and unzip it into your site folder. The ZIP contains the loader, the cores, and a data directory, no installer, no build step.

If you'd rather not self-host, the project's own demo page shows the same setup; the steps below work identically on any static host.

### 2. Add your own games

Create a folder (call it `roms`) and copy in only ROMs you dumped from games you own, plus homebrew or public-domain ROMs. One subfolder per system keeps cores straight, `roms/gba/`, `roms/snes/`, and so on.

Name files clearly. EmulatorJS doesn't care about fancy naming schemes; it cares that the file is a valid dump.

### 3. Embed the player

Drop this into an HTML page where you want the game to appear:

<div id="game"></div>
<script>
  EJS_player = '#game';
  EJS_core = 'gba';                 // the core for your system
  EJS_gameUrl = 'roms/gba/mygame.gba'; // a ROM you dumped yourself
  EJS_pathtodata = 'data/';          // EmulatorJS data directory
</script>
<script src="data/loader.js"></script>

Swap `EJS_core` for the system you're playing (`snes`, `nes`, `gb`, `gba`, `n64`, `nds`, and more are supported). The full core list is in the project's documentation.

### 4. BIOS files (dump your own)

Some cores refuse to boot without a system BIOS. Dump the BIOS from hardware you own, the same dumpers in the rip-your-own guide usually handle this, and place it where the core's documentation says to look. Never download a BIOS file; like ROMs, they're copyrighted software.

### 5. Extras worth knowing

- Gamepad support is built in; most USB and Bluetooth controllers just work
- Save states live in the browser; export them if you switch devices
- Netplay is available for some cores if you want online multiplayer
- On mobile, add the page to your home screen for a near-native feel

### The rule, one more time

EmulatorJS gives you the player, not the games. If a setup tutorial tells you to download a ROM pack, close the tab, that tutorial is pointing you at piracy. Your library should be: dumps of games you physically own, homebrew from its authors, and public-domain releases. That's the whole legal lane, and it's plenty.

## RetroArch setup guide
Difficulty: Beginner · ~20 min · slug: retroarch-setup

Install RetroArch, add cores for hardware you own, and load your own dumped games, controllers, save states, shaders, and netplay included.

### What it is (and the legal line)

RetroArch is a free, open-source frontend for emulators. Instead of one emulator per system, you install RetroArch once and add small emulator modules called cores, one for each console you want to play. It runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and even in a browser.

RetroArch contains no games and no BIOS files. You bring those: dumps of games you own (see the rip-your-own guide) and homebrew or public-domain titles.

### 1. Install RetroArch

Download RetroArch from retroarch.com, pick your platform. It's also on Steam and most package managers, which handle updates for you. Install it like any normal app; the first launch walks you through the basics.

### 2. Download cores (the emulators)

Go to Main Menu → Online Updater → Core Downloader. You'll see a list of cores, each named for the hardware it emulates. Install the core matching hardware you own, for example, a Game Boy Advance core if you have GBA cartridges to dump.

Cores are emulator software, and they're legal. Installing ten cores you never use harms nothing; loading a game you don't own into one is the part that's piracy.

### 3. Load your own games

Main Menu → Load Content → browse to your dumped ROM file. RetroArch will ask which core to use; pick the one you installed. To build a pretty library view, use Import Content → Scan Directory on a folder of your dumps: RetroArch matches them against its database and builds per-system playlists with box art.

### 4. Controllers

Settings → Input. Most USB and Bluetooth gamepads are recognized automatically with sane default mappings, plug in and play. If a button feels wrong, remap it per-core under Quick Menu → Controls while a game is running; RetroArch saves the remap for that core.

### 5. The good stuff: saves, shaders, netplay

- Save states: Quick Menu → Save State, with slots per game
- Rewind: enable it in Settings → Frame Throttle, then hold the rewind hotkey to scrub mistakes away
- Shaders: Quick Menu → Shaders adds CRT scanlines and other retro looks
- Netplay: Netplay menu for online multiplayer on supported cores
- Achievements: sign up at retroachievements.org and link it in Settings for retro achievements

### The rule, one more time

Keep your library to three sources: dumps of games you own, homebrew from its authors, and public-domain releases. RetroArch never asks where your files came from, that's your responsibility, and it's the whole difference between a legal retro setup and a piracy box.

## GBA-to-WASM recompiler guide
Difficulty: Advanced · ~90 min · slug: gba-to-wasm-recompiler

Turn a GBA cartridge you own into a self-contained browser page via static recompilation, the user-supplied-ROMs-only pattern, end to end.

### The pattern

Most browser emulation interprets a console's CPU in real time. A static recompiler takes a different path: it translates the game's ARM/Thumb machine code into WebAssembly ahead of time, once. The result is a self-contained web page: WASM plus a small runtime shim, that plays the game with no emulator needed at runtime.

The open-source demo at agnt-gg/gba-pokemon-rom-to-wasm walks the whole pattern end to end and is the best reference for how the pieces fit.

### The non-negotiable input rule

The input ROM must be a dump of a cartridge you physically own, see the rip-your-own-cartridges guide. Two hard rules:

1. Never feed a downloaded ROM into the toolchain. The recompiler doesn't care where the file came from; the law does.
2. Don't redistribute the built page. The output still contains the original game's copyrighted code, so sharing the build is sharing the game.

Build for yourself, play it yourself. That's the legal lane.

### 1. Dump your own cartridge

Use a cartridge dumper, a GB Operator, Joey Jr., Sanni Cart Reader, or similar, to read your own GBA cartridge into a ROM file on your computer. Verify the dump (most dumper software shows a checksum) before you build.

### 2. Run the recompiler on your dump

Clone the recompiler repository and follow its README for the toolchain install. Point the build script at your dumped ROM file. The build emits three things: a WASM module with your game's translated code, the JavaScript glue and runtime shim (this implements the GBA's graphics, sound, and timer hardware), and an HTML shell that loads it all.

### 3. Host the build yourself

The output is static files, so any static web host works, or just open the HTML file locally. Saves typically persist via localStorage or IndexedDB in the browser. Keep the page private, or share it only with people who own the same cartridge.

### How it works, briefly

At build time, each ARM instruction in the game maps to equivalent WebAssembly operations. Anything the game expects from real GBA hardware, the picture processing unit, the sound channels, the timers, the memory-mapped I/O, is implemented in the runtime shim the recompiler ships with. It's emulation, just done ahead of time instead of on the fly.

### Limits and gotchas

- Not every game recompiles cleanly; anti-piracy checks and unusual hardware tricks can break the build
- Performance varies by browser and device; desktop Chrome/Firefox are the smoothest targets
- Debugging a broken build means reading the recompiler's logs, not the game's code, start with a simple, well-documented game
- This pattern generalizes: the same idea applies to other consoles, with different recompiler projects

## Rip-your-own-cartridges guide
Difficulty: Beginner · ~45 min · slug: rip-your-own-cartridges

Turn cartridges you own into verified ROM backups with a USB dumper, hardware picks, the dumping ritual, and the no-distribution rule.

### The idea

Dumping is reading the data off a cartridge or disc you own into a file on your computer. That file, the ROM or disc image, is a backup of your property, and it's the only legal way to get game files for the emulators and recompilers in the other guides.

This guide is practical how-to, not legal advice. The general principle is simple: back up what you own, and never distribute the copies.

### The legal framing (general principles)

Making a personal backup of software you own is treated very differently from downloading or sharing copies you have no rights to. The bright line is distribution: uploading your dumps, sharing them with friends, or downloading someone else's is piracy regardless of whether you own the game.

Laws vary by country and change over time. When in doubt, the conservative read, your dumps, your devices, no sharing, keeps you safe everywhere.

### Pick a dumper for your system

- Game Boy / Game Boy Color / Game Boy Advance: GB Operator (Epilogue) or Joey Jr., dead simple USB dumpers
- SNES + Genesis: Retrode 2, plug the cart into a USB adapter that mounts like a drive
- Multi-system DIY: INLretro Dumper or the open-source Sanni Cart Reader, more systems, more tinkering
- Save files: most of these dumpers also back up the save RAM, so your 100-hour file survives

### The dumping ritual

1. Clean the cartridge's edge connector with isopropyl alcohol and a cotton swab, dirty contacts cause bad dumps
2. Seat the cart firmly in the dumper
3. Run the dumper software and save the ROM file
4. Verify it: good dumper software shows a checksum. Compare it against a known-good database entry for your exact cartridge, a match means a perfect read
5. Keep the physical cartridge. It's your proof of ownership and the reason the backup is yours to make

### Disc-based games

Optical media needs a compatible disc drive plus dumping software; the per-system guides in preservation communities document exact drive models and settings. The same rule applies: your disc, your dump, no sharing. Disc dumps are big, budget storage accordingly.

### Store it right

- Keep each ROM next to a small text file with its checksum and the cartridge it came from
- Back up save files separately; they're tiny and irreplaceable
- Store everything twice (local drive + a backup), dumped once, kept forever
- Label homebrew and public-domain ROMs as such so your future self knows what's shareable

## Homebrew & public-domain sources
Difficulty: Reference · ~10 min · slug: homebrew-and-public-domain

Where to find legal homebrew ROMs and public-domain games: archives, dev communities, itch.io, and open-source originals.

### What counts as legal

Homebrew means new games made by hobbyists for old (and new) hardware, released free by their authors. Public domain means the copyright expired or was explicitly waived. Both are fully legal to download, play, and share, they're the guilt-free way to fill an emulator library or a recompiler project.

### Where to find them

- pdroms.de, a long-running archive of homebrew ROMs across dozens of systems. Everything there is distributed by its authors.
- nesdev.com, the NES homebrew development community: forums, tutorials, and released homebrew games.
- gbdev.io, the Game Boy homebrew hub: dev resources plus finished, free games.
- itch.io (itch.io/games, search 'homebrew'), many homebrew devs release ROMs free on their itch pages; filter by 'play in browser' for instant play.
- Internet Archive collections, the MS-DOS Games, Internet Arcade, and Console Living Room collections (all in our game directory) include homebrew and public-domain titles; check each item's rights statement.

### Open-source originals (not ROMs at all)

- OpenTTD (openttd.org), a complete, open-source transport sim and a genuinely great game
- The open-source web games in our directory: 2048, Hextris, A Dark Room, and friends are free software you can also self-host
- Engine recreations exist for some classics, but they typically need original game data from a copy you own, the engine is free, the assets aren't

### The smell test

If a 'homebrew' site also offers commercial ROM downloads, leave. The test is simple: does the site point you at the game's author, or at a download button for a game Nintendo still sells? Link the guide and the tool, never the pirated content. When in doubt, the author's own page wins.

## How GBA becomes WebAssembly
Difficulty: Intermediate · ~12 min · slug: gba-wasm

The reverse-engineering pattern behind browser GBA: ARM/THUMB basic blocks lifted into real WASM, frame timing, memory mapping, original explainer.

### The CPU problem: ARM in a browser

The GBA runs on an ARM7TDMI with ARM and THUMB instruction sets. Recompilers translate the game's machine code into WebAssembly ahead of time, so the browser runs it natively instead of interpreting it.

### Basic blocks: the unit of translation

Straight-line runs of instructions become individual WASM functions; ARM registers become WASM locals; branches become a dispatch loop. Self-modifying code is handled by checksumming and retranslating.

### Memory mapping: faking the hardware

A flat WASM memory block gets a memory map on top: hardware addresses route to implementations of the PPU, sound channels, DMA, and timers. BIOS calls are reimplemented clean-room (HLE).

### Frame timing

The GBA runs at exactly 59.73 fps; the runtime paces translated code against the display and audio clocks so games run at true speed.

### Differential verification

Serious projects run the WASM translation and a trusted interpreter side by side and compare CPU state after every block, any divergence is a translation bug.

## How emulation works
Difficulty: Beginner · ~8 min · slug: how-emulation-works

Plain-English explainer: interpreters vs. recompilers, cycle accuracy, what a BIOS does, save states, and why the browser is enough now.

### The core idea

An emulator pretends to be the original chips: CPU, graphics, sound, timers, well enough that the game can't tell the difference.

### Interpreters vs. recompilers

Interpreters simulate one instruction at a time (simple, slower); recompilers translate chunks to native code ahead of time (complex, faster).

### Cycle accuracy

Old games race the hardware beam; cycle-accurate emulators simulate chips in lockstep so timing tricks work.

### What a BIOS does

Some consoles need firmware dumped from your own hardware; others (GBA via mGBA) reimplement it clean-room; some need none.

### Save states

Complete snapshots of the emulated machine, save mid-jump. In browsers they persist via local storage / IndexedDB.

## Best emulator per system
Difficulty: Reference · ~6 min · slug: best-emulator-per-system

One honest emulator pick per classic system: accuracy, ease of use, platform notes. Software only, no ROM links.

### The picks

mGBA (GBA), SameBoy (GB/GBC), Mesen (NES), Snes9x (SNES), Genesis Plus GX (Genesis), Mupen64Plus-Next (N64), DuckStation (PSX, needs your BIOS), PCSX2 (PS2, needs your BIOS), PPSSPP (PSP), melonDS (NDS), RetroArch (everything), EmulatorJS (in-browser).

### How to choose

Play in a tab: this site's Player. One system: the standalone pick. Many systems: RetroArch. Accuracy above all: Mesen, SameBoy, mGBA.

## Game Boy Advance emulation guide
Difficulty: Beginner · ~12 min · slug: gba

The Player's gba core is mGBA (verified backend, the single GBA backend in the EmulatorJS core list). BIOS-free. Covers the settings that matter (color correction, fast-forward, Keep in Browser), save states/cheats wired to Player 2.0, a Player deep link (player.html?core=gba), and a curl-verified homebrew starter pack.

### The core: mGBA, the accuracy king

The Player's gba core is mGBA, the single GBA backend in the official EmulatorJS core list, and one of the most accurate GBA emulators ever written. Auto-detected from .gba files; the manual dropdown exists only if detection fails.

### BIOS notes

None needed. mGBA reimplements the GBA BIOS calls from scratch (clean-room HLE), so the core boots with no BIOS file at all.

### Settings that matter

Color correction (GBA games were drawn for the dim unlit screen, correction restores the intended look); fast-forward for slow stretches; Keep in Browser under Settings -> Save States so the Player 2.0 Save tool can export/import states as files.

### Performance

The lightest system in the Player. Any laptop, desktop, tablet, or phone from the last decade runs full speed. Stutter means browser throttling (tabs, low-power mode), not the core.

### Saves & cheats

Save states from the in-game menu; in-game battery saves persist automatically. Player 2.0 Cheats tool takes GameShark/Action Replay v3 codes, stored per game and injected before boot (EJS_cheats). Player 2.0 Controls tool remaps Player 1 keyboard/gamepad; applies on next boot.

### Homebrew starter pack

pdroms.de GBA section (https://pdroms.de/nintendo-game-boy-advance-gba); itch.io games tagged Game Boy Advance (https://itch.io/games/tag-game-boy-advance); GameBrew's list of all GBA homebrew (https://gamebrew.org/wiki/List_of_all_GBA_homebrew). All verified live 2026-10-11.

## SNES emulation guide
Difficulty: Beginner · ~12 min · slug: snes

The Player's snes core is Snes9x (default SNES backend in the EmulatorJS core list; bsnes is the alternate for accuracy purists). BIOS-free. Covers hi-res blending, sound buffer/latency, save states and Game Genie/Pro Action Replay cheats via Player 2.0, deep link (player.html?core=snes), and a verified homebrew starter pack.

### The core: Snes9x, the workhorse

The Player's snes core is Snes9x, the default SNES backend in the official EmulatorJS core list (alternate: bsnes). In development since 1997; handles Super FX, SA-1, and DSP chips well. Auto-detected from .sfc/.smc files.

### BIOS notes

None needed, the SNES has no separate system BIOS; every cartridge is self-contained.

### Settings that matter

Hi-res blending for Mode 7/transparency effects; sound buffer/latency tuning for crackle vs. lag; fast-forward for slow JRPG intros; Keep in Browser for the Player 2.0 Save tool.

### Performance

Trivial on anything: 1990 hardware on a 1997-hardened core. Slowdown is browser throttling, never the core.

### Saves & cheats

Save states via the in-game menu (export/import/delete with the Player 2.0 Save tool); SRAM battery saves persist. Cheats tool takes Game Genie and Pro Action Replay codes, stored per game, injected before boot.

### Homebrew starter pack

pdroms.de SNES section (https://pdroms.de/super-nintendo-snes-super-famicom); itch.io tag-super-nintendo (https://itch.io/games/tag-super-nintendo); itch.io tag-snes (https://itch.io/games/tag-snes). All verified live 2026-10-11.

### Accuracy purists: bsnes

bsnes favors cycle-level accuracy over speed for the handful of games that need it; it's the EmulatorJS alternate SNES backend for self-hosted setups. Snes9x covers essentially everything in browser play.

## NES emulation guide
Difficulty: Beginner · ~10 min · slug: nes

The Player's nes core is FCEUmm (default NES backend in the EmulatorJS core list; Nestopia UE is the alternate for accuracy purists). BIOS-free for cartridges, the one exception is Famicom Disk System disks, which need a BIOS dumped from your own hardware. Covers mapper support, the sprite-flicker switch, save states and Game Genie cheats via Player 2.0, deep link (player.html?core=nes), and a verified homebrew starter pack.

### The core: FCEUmm, the mapper sponge

The Player's nes core is FCEUmm, the default NES backend in the official EmulatorJS core list (alternate: Nestopia UE). The NES put half its hardware in the cartridge (the mapper chips), and FCEUmm's whole reputation is supporting hundreds of them. Auto-detected from .nes files.

### BIOS notes

None needed for cartridges, the NES has no system BIOS. The single exception: Famicom Disk System .fds disks need the FDS BIOS, dumped from your own Famicom hardware. Never download one.

### Settings that matter

The no-sprite-limit option trades the NES's famous 8-sprites-per-line flicker for a cleaner picture some games weren't drawn for; palette choice is taste, not accuracy homework; fast-forward for slow RPG text; Keep in Browser for the Player 2.0 Save tool.

### Performance

Effortless: 1983 hardware. If an NES game stutters in the browser, the browser is throttling the tab, not the core struggling.

### Saves & cheats

Save states via the in-game menu (export/import/delete with the Player 2.0 Save tool); battery saves persist. Cheats tool takes Game Genie codes, the NES is the system the Game Genie was invented for, stored per game, injected before boot.

### Homebrew starter pack

Zophar's Domain NES public-domain shelf (https://zophar.net/pdroms/nes.html); itch.io NES + NESmaker tag (https://itch.io/games/tag-nes/tag-nesmaker); itch.io neshomebrew tag (https://itch.io/games/newest/tag-neshomebrew). All verified live 2026-10-12.

### Accuracy purists: Nestopia UE

Nestopia UE favors cycle-level accuracy, the pick for finicky mappers and timing-sensitive homebrew. It's the EmulatorJS alternate NES backend for self-hosted setups. FCEUmm covers essentially everything in browser play.

## Nintendo 64 emulation guide
Difficulty: Intermediate · ~15 min · slug: n64

The Player's n64 core is Mupen64Plus-Next (default N64 backend in the EmulatorJS core list; alternate Parallel-N64). BIOS-free. Honest about per-game quirks and real hardware requirements: framebuffer emulation fixes most games, internal resolution is the performance lever, weak devices should pick SNES/GBA instead. Deep link (player.html?core=n64) and verified homebrew starter pack.

### The core: Mupen64Plus-Next

The Player's n64 core is Mupen64Plus-Next, the default N64 backend in the official EmulatorJS core list. The N64's graphics quirks make it the least predictable system here: most games run great, a few famous ones have graphical oddities. Auto-detected from .n64/.z64/.v64.

### BIOS notes

None needed for the browser core, it boots games with no BIOS file.

### Settings that matter

Framebuffer emulation is the biggest compatibility knob (fixes broken menus/textures); internal resolution is the biggest performance knob (lower it first when stuttering); texture filtering is cheap taste; analog sticks beat keyboards for this system.

### Performance

Honest requirements: a recent laptop/desktop for full speed in a browser; older Chromebooks, weak tablets, and old phones struggle. Lower internal resolution to native, close tabs, disable low-power mode.

### Saves & cheats

Save states from the in-game menu (export/import with the Player 2.0 Save tool); the engine emulates the memory pak so in-game saves work. Cheats tool takes GameShark codes, treat as experimental on N64. Analog-stick axes need the engine's own Control Settings, not the Player remap tool.

### Homebrew starter pack

pdroms.de N64 section (https://pdroms.de/nintendo-64-n64); itch.io tag-nintendo-64 (https://itch.io/games/tag-nintendo-64); n64.dev community (https://n64.dev/). All verified live 2026-10-11.

## PlayStation emulation guide
Difficulty: Intermediate · ~15 min · slug: ps1

The Player's psx core is PCSX-ReARMed (default PSX backend in the EmulatorJS core list; alternate Mednafen PSX HW). BIOS honesty: boots via HLE with no BIOS, but a user-dumped scph BIOS improves accuracy (never download one). Covers enhanced resolution, fast-load, saves/cheats via Player 2.0, deep link (player.html?core=psx), and a verified homebrew starter pack.

### The core: PCSX-ReARMed

The Player's psx core is PCSX-ReARMed, the default PlayStation backend in the official EmulatorJS core list. Fast enough for browsers, accurate enough for most of the library. Detects .cue/.bin/.iso/.img/.chd/.m3u; use .m3u playlists for multi-disc games.

### BIOS notes: honest, not scary

Boots most games with no BIOS via built-in HLE (high-level firmware reimplementation). A handful of games glitch without genuine firmware, the proper fix is dumping the BIOS from your own PlayStation and attaching it with the Player's BIOS picker. Never download a BIOS file.

### Settings that matter

Enhanced resolution (2x is the sweet spot); CD fast-load/fast boot; dithering (taste, purists leave it on); analog toggle for DualShock-supported games.

### Performance

Lighter than its reputation: recent laptops/desktops and recent phones run full speed. Stutter fixes: drop enhanced resolution to 1x, close tabs, exit low-power mode. Keep own rips as .chd, much smaller.

### Saves & cheats

Save states via the in-game menu (export/import with the Player 2.0 Save tool); memory-card saves work normally. Cheats tool takes GameShark codes, stored per game, injected before boot.

### Homebrew starter pack

pdroms.de PS1 section (https://pdroms.de/sony-playstation-ps1); itch.io tag-playstation (https://itch.io/games/tag-playstation); PSXDEV community (https://psxdev.net/); psx.dev hub (https://psx.dev/). All verified live 2026-10-11.

### Prefer a desktop app? DuckStation

DuckStation (duckstation.org) is the modern PS1 accuracy pick with gorgeous upscaling; it needs your own dumped BIOS for full accuracy. The browser Player wins on zero-setup convenience.

## Make games for dead consoles: the homebrew development primer
Difficulty: Intermediate · ~25 min · slug: homebrew-development

Write your own games for the GBA, Game Boy, and NES: the honest toolchain (devkitARM, RGBDS, cc65), how to learn the hardware via Tonc and gbdev.io, testing on emulators and flash carts, and shipping through jams, itch.io, and showcases.

### Why dead consoles are the friendliest dev targets

Fixed hardware means zero surprises: one CPU, one screen, identical for every player. Constraints force design over decoration, and the feedback loop is minutes. The scene ships real games yearly, from jam entries to releases like 2026's Zombie Nest GBA and the MAGFest Indie Retro Homebrew Showcase finalists.

### Pick your first system (the honest ladder)

GBA first (C, real compiler, the Tonc tutorial, forgiving CPU), then Game Boy/Color (LR35902, great gbdev.io community), then NES (6502, mappers as the boss fight). SNES/Genesis/N64 come after you've shipped something small.

### The GBA toolchain, end to end

devkitPro + devkitARM: install the package manager, run `sudo dkp-pacman -S gba-dev gba-examples`, set DEVKITPRO/DEVKITARM/PATH, copy /opt/devkitpro/examples/gba/template, run make. A .gba with no errors means the toolchain works, one evening, start to finish.

### Learn the hardware: Tonc and the 240x160 canvas

Tonc (coranac.com/tonc/text/) is the canonical GBA course: video modes, tiles and sprites, 15-bit palettes, the vblank heartbeat. libgba vs libtonc vs the Butano engine, pick libtonc as a beginner.

### The 8-bit path: Game Boy and NES

Game Boy: RGBDS (assembler, the pro path) or GBDK-2020 (C, friendlier), Pan Docs as the hardware bible, Homebrew Hub (hh.gbdev.io) to study what shipped. NES: cc65/ca65 for the 6502; start on mapper 0 (NROM). Scope discipline: ship a tiny finished game, not a dead epic.

### Test like it's 2001

Develop on mGBA (accurate, great debugger), validate on real hardware via flash cartridges. Watch for emulator-masked bugs: uninitialized memory, timing assumptions, DMA misuse.

### Ship it: jams, itch.io, and showcases

Game jams (GBA Jam entries), itch.io with correct system tags and free/pay-what-you-want ROMs, MAGFest's Indie Retro Homebrew Showcase, and physical cartridge runs for standouts. Play others' homebrew first via the homebrew sources guide.

### The legal lane for developers

Your code, your art, your music, never lift commercial assets. Open-source the engine if you like; clones of mechanics are legal, copies of assets aren't; fan games with others' characters live in a takedown gray zone. Every byte yours = sell, share, jam, press.

## Play together online: the netplay guide
Difficulty: Intermediate · ~20 min · slug: netplay

Retro multiplayer over the internet: how RetroArch's rewind-based rollback netplay works, the same-version-same-core-same-game rule, hosting via lobby/relay/port-forward, what plays well (8/16-bit) and what doesn't (PS1/N64, link cables), plus Dolphin's 2026 Android netplay.

### What netplay actually sends

Not video, controller inputs, a few bytes per frame. Both players run the same emulator, core, and game locally; identical inputs keep both screens in agreement. Everyone still needs their own legal copy.

### How RetroArch's rollback works

Replay-based: your game runs ahead with zero added input delay; when the other player's inputs arrive late, the emulator rewinds to the last agreed frame and replays with the real inputs, invisibly. Up to 16 players plus spectators.

### The matching rule: same, same, same

Same RetroArch version (1.22.2 current), same core version, byte-identical game content on every machine. No save states mid-session, the top two desync causes are content mismatch and mid-game states.

### Hosting: lobby, relay, or port forward

Host loads the game, Start Netplay Host; clients Connect to Netplay Host or use the lobby browser. Relay servers = zero router config but extra latency; forwarding TCP 55435 = fastest. Official docs: retroarch.com netplay page + libretro netplay docs.

### What plays well (and what doesn't)

Excellent: NES/SNES/Genesis/GBA/FBNeo arcade. Impractical: PS1/N64 (serialization too slow). Not emulated: link cables, no Pokemon trading over netplay; exceptions are the TGB-Dual and SameBoy cores for same-game GB/GBC multiplayer.

### New in 2026: Dolphin on your phone

Dolphin 2609 (Sept 2026) added Android NetPlay with lockstep networking against desktop clients, cross-platform GameCube/Wii multiplayer, phone to PC. Dolphin is now on the Google Play Store too.

### Netplay on this site: the honest state

EmulatorJS advertises experimental WebRTC room-code netplay but it is unverified on the stable build, not enabled here, not promised. What works today: hot-seat multi-gamepad play, the Party Planner for couch rotations, and tournament brackets.

### Troubleshooting checklist

Desync at start = content mismatch (compare checksums). Desync mid-session = save state loaded or core versions differ. 'Failed to initialize' = wrong IP/host not hosting/firewall. Stutter = wrong system for rollback or relay latency. Delayed inputs = network distance.

## Saves that survive: states, SRAM & backup workflows
Difficulty: Beginner · ~12 min · slug: save-workflows

Save states vs. battery saves vs. memory cards: what each one is, where it lives in RetroArch and in this site's Player (IndexedDB, Keep in Browser, named slots), moving saves between emulators, and the 3-2-1 backup routine.

### The three save machines

Save states = the emulator's full-machine snapshot. Battery saves (SRAM) = the game's own save system, faithfully emulated. Memory cards/controller paks = disc-era external storage as image files. States are the emulator's snapshots, SRAM is the game's diary, cards are the filing cabinet.

### Save states: snapshots of everything

Most powerful, most fragile: version-tied (won't cross emulator versions/cores) and all-or-nothing. Discipline: states for convenience, SRAM for permanence; export important states as files before emulator updates.

### Battery saves: the game's own memory

SRAM emulated as a file (often .srm). Portable between emulators and flash carts, the closest thing to a universal save format. Close games cleanly so SRAM flushes; dump SRAM with your cartridges since the 100-hour file is irreplaceable.

### Memory cards & controller paks

Card images (.mcr for PS1.mpk-ish for N64 paks) behave like the plastic. Per-game cards avoid the 'card full' tragedy; back up the card file like any save. Original hardware paks had batteries that die too.

### Where RetroArch keeps it all

Savefiles dir (SRAM + card images, the folder to back up), Savestates dir (numbered slots), SaveRAM autosave interval (flush every N seconds, turn it on), state slot hotkeys.

### Where this site's Player keeps it all

Default: the engine downloads states as .state files. Keep in Browser mode: states in IndexedDB (EmulatorJS-states store), unlocking named slots (save/restore/rename/export/delete) and 1/5/15-min auto-save. Browser storage is mortal, export what you care about.

### Moving saves between emulators

SRAM (.srm): usually portable, rename to match and it works. States: never portable across cores/versions/emulators, convert via in-game save first. Memory cards: portable within shared formats. Region must match.

### The backup routine (3-2-1)

Three copies, two media, one off-site: working copy, a dated saves-backup folder, cloud/external drive. Include SRAM, card images, exported states, and a note of the emulator version. Saves are kilobytes, no excuses.

## Make pixels look right: CRT shaders & display science
Difficulty: Intermediate · ~10 min · slug: crt-shaders-display

Why retro games look wrong on modern screens, the anatomy of the CRT look (scanlines, grille, glow), shader presets from zfast-crt to crt-royale, integer vs. bilinear scaling, and the honest science of input lag, run-ahead, and refresh rates.

### The problem: drawn for a screen you don't own

Pixel artists painted for CRT blur: composite smear, phosphor bleed, scanlines. Dithering was drawn to melt into new colors on a CRT, raw LCD pixels expose the trick. Shaders put the display back.

### Anatomy of the CRT look

Five stacked effects: scanlines, aperture grille (Trinitron stripes) vs. shadow mask (dot triads), phosphor glow/bloom (melts dithering), curvature/vignette, NTSC artifacting. Good shaders model all five.

### Shaders: the look, recreated

RetroArch: Quick Menu -> Shaders -> Load Shader Preset. Families: slang (Vulkan/D3D), glsl (OpenGL), cg (legacy). Ladder: zfast-crt (cheap default), crt-easymode, crt-guest-advanced (tunable favorite), crt-royale (reference, heavy). Taste, not correctness.

### The scaling problem (integer vs. blur)

Integer scaling = whole-pixel multiples, even pixels, black borders. Bilinear = fills screen, shimmer on scroll. The Player has an integer-scale toggle; pair with the CRT overlay for sharp pixels + soft light.

### Input lag: the honest numbers

One frame = 16.7ms at 60Hz. Chain: emulator ~1 frame, TV processing 1-3+ frames without Game Mode (the big one), wireless controllers a few ms, v-sync up to 1 frame. Fixes in order: Game Mode, wired controller, emulator tricks.

### Run-ahead & black frame insertion

Run-ahead: emulator simulates 1-2 frames ahead and rolls back, deletes emulator latency, needs a deterministic core, can't fix TV lag. BFI: strobes black frames for CRT-like motion clarity; halves brightness, needs 120Hz+.

### Refresh rates: 59.73 vs. 60

GBA runs 59.73fps, SNES ~60.09Hz, PAL 50Hz; displays run exactly 60/120/144. Mismatch = periodic duplicated/dropped frames. Answers: ignore it, variable refresh rate (G-Sync/FreeSync), or matching display modes.

### The practical recipe

Game Mode on, integer scaling or a light CRT preset, wired controller, 1 frame of run-ahead in RetroArch for 8/16-bit cores. Then stop tuning and play.

## Retro games for every player: an accessibility guide
Difficulty: Beginner · ~8 min · slug: accessibility-in-retro-gaming

Old games shipped zero accessibility features, the emulator layer adds what they lack: remapping, turbo/autofire, rewind, save states, color correction, and honest difficulty options. No medical claims, just the toolbox.

### The honest baseline

1991 games: no remapping, no colorblind mode, no subtitles, no difficulty slider. The good news: emulator-added tools work on the whole library at once. No medical claims here, a toolbox, not a diagnosis.

### Hands: remapping, turbo, one-handed play

Remap everything (the Player's per-system Controls tool; RetroArch per core). Turbo/autofire replaces button-mashing with a setting. One-handed layouts via full remapping; RPGs and puzzlers are friendliest. Mix keyboard + gamepad freely.

### Eyes: color, contrast, and size

GBA color correction restores intended contrast; OS color filters apply to emulator windows; integer scaling + fullscreen for size; drop shaders before anything else if text is hard to read; retro games flash a lot, preview first, keep sessions short.

### Ears: what sound actually carries

Retro games carry almost nothing critical in audio, no voice acting, no audio-only objectives. One of the most naturally accessible catalogs for deaf/hard-of-hearing players; rhythm games are the exception.

### Mind: difficulty is a dial now

Save states, rewind (RetroArch), slow motion, cheat codes as accessibility tools, guides/walkthroughs for cryptic 90s design. Old difficulty was often artificial, the dial is legitimate.

### On 'cheating' (it's not)

Assists don't diminish the game; the 1991 developers aren't grading you. Finishing with assists beats bouncing off with pride. The only wrong way to play is the way that makes you stop.

### This site's own commitments

Keyboard-operable everything, reduced-motion respected (kids corner disables motion unconditionally), semantic landmarks + skip links + aria-live, high-contrast palette, mobile-first. Barriers found = bugs.

### Where to go next

The Player (remap/cheats/slots/display), RetroArch setup guide (turbo/rewind), CRT & display guide (readability tuning), parent guide, kids corner.

## Keep your games forever: the preservation guide
Difficulty: Intermediate · ~20 min · slug: preserving-your-games

Archive your own library properly: checksums (CRC32/SHA-1), No-Intro and Redump verification, the modern redumper/MPF/OmniDrive disc-dumping stack, lossless CHD compression, ROM managers and DAT files, and the 3-2-1 backup rule.

### Why bother: the quiet crisis

Media dies: save batteries (15-20 years), disc rot, extinct dumping drives. ~87% of pre-2010 US games are out of print (VGHF reissue-market survey). A verified dump of your own copy is a game that survives.

### The legal frame (brief, honest)

Not legal advice: personal backups of what you own vs. distribution, the bright line. Context: the 2024 DMCA rulemaking rejected remote sharing of out-of-print games by archives; next cycle 2027. Your personal archiving doesn't depend on it.

### Checksums: the fingerprint

CRC32/SHA-1: one changed byte, totally different hash. Compute via 7-Zip/certutil (Windows) or shasum (macOS/Linux); compare against the database entry for your exact game+region. Store the checksum in a text file next to the ROM.

### No-Intro: the cartridge database

DAT-o-matic catalogs every known-good cartridge dump. Naming: Title (Region), (Rev N), [!] = verified good dump, [b] = bad, [o] = overdump, (Unl) = unlicensed. Name files this way; managers and scrapers do the rest.

### Redump: the disc database

redump.org catalogs disc systems. Realities: compatible drive required (Plextor/Lite-On historically; OmniDrive firmware, March 2026, expanded Blu-ray drive support incl. Xbox/GameCube/Wii); modern stack is redumper + MPF (SabreTools), DiscImageCreator for GD-ROM; checksums cover raw 2352-byte sectors. Active project, tens of thousands of discs.

### Compress without losing a byte

CHD (via chdman) for discs: 30-50% smaller, lossless, emulators load it directly. 7z for cartridges (hash the extracted file when verifying). Rule: compress for storage, verify from originals.

### ROM managers & DAT files

clrmamepro/RomVault + No-Intro/Redump DAT files: verify, auto-rename, flag bad dumps and duplicates. 1G1R (one game, one ROM) for intentional curation.

### The 3-2-1 archive

Three copies, two media, one off-site: working library, external drive with checksums, cloud/relative's house. Re-verify checksums yearly (bit rot is real); migrate media every ~5 years. Dump it, checksum it, name it, compress a copy, keep three, check yearly.

## Controllers in the browser: the gamepad setup guide
Difficulty: Beginner · ~20 min · slug: gamepad-setup

Get any USB or Bluetooth controller working with browser games and this site's Player, the Gamepad API, testing, per-system remapping, and honest troubleshooting.

### Why a controller changes browser games

Some games were designed around a pad, and it shows. Platformers, racers, twin-stick shooters, and fighting games all play better with analog sticks and real buttons than with arrow keys, and anything you play in this site's Player (the EmulatorJS console) was literally built for a controller. The good news: modern browsers speak gamepad natively. No drivers, no mapping software, no downloads, plug in and play.

### How browser gamepads work (the 60-second version)

Browsers expose controllers through the Gamepad API: a page asks for the list of connected pads with navigator.getGamepads(), and the browser fires gamepadconnected / gamepaddisconnected events when pads come and go. Each pad reports buttons as pressed-or-not values and sticks as axes between -1 and 1. Most controllers follow the 'standard' mapping, which means button 0 is the bottom face button (A on Xbox, Cross on PlayStation) no matter which brand you plugged in. The W3C Gamepad spec and MDN's Gamepad API docs cover the details if you're building something yourself.

### Pick your controller

- Xbox (One / Series), the safe default. Wired over USB or Bluetooth; the standard mapping just works everywhere.
- PlayStation (DualShock 4 / DualSense), excellent pads, work wired or over Bluetooth; some browsers show PlayStation button labels, some show Xbox-style numbers. The positions are identical.
- Switch Pro Controller, works over Bluetooth and USB; check the button mapping in a tester first, since its face layout is swapped vs. Xbox.
- 8BitDo and other Bluetooth pads, usually fine; their 'X-input mode' (the Xbox-compatible mode) is the one browsers understand best.
- Cheap no-name USB pads, often fine for 2D games; test every button before a tournament.

### Connect it: USB vs. Bluetooth

USB is the zero-fuss path: plug the cable in and the browser sees the pad within a second. For Bluetooth, put the controller in pairing mode (Xbox: hold the pair button; DualSense: hold PS + Create; 8BitDo: hold the mode-specific combo from its manual), then pair it in your OS Bluetooth settings like any device. One honest caveat: some Bluetooth stacks add a few milliseconds of input lag, imperceptible in RPGs and platformers, worth knowing about for rhythm games and fighters. If a pad refuses to appear, try the cable before anything else.

### Test it before you play

Open html5gamepad.com with the controller connected and press buttons: you should see each input light up with its standard-mapping number. This one page answers every 'is it the game or the pad?' question in ten seconds. If the tester sees the pad but a game doesn't, the game probably only polls for pads on a timer or needs a button press to 'wake' the listing, click into the game and press any button. If the tester doesn't see it either, it's a connection problem, not a game problem.

### Gamepads in this site's Player

The Player (this site's EmulatorJS console) has gamepad support built in: Player 1's pad just works, no setup. For finer control, the per-system remapper (Player 2.1) lets you capture gamepad buttons per system: open the remap panel, pick a button, and press the pad button you want. Your mapping is stored per system in the browser and applied at boot. Note it overrides any mapping you set inside the engine's own menu, and Esc cancels a capture. If your pad has a non-standard layout, capture each button once and you're done forever.

### Which catalog games love a pad

Reach for the controller for: the arcade shelf (Robotron: 2084 is the twin-stick original; Defender and Joust were built for arcade sticks), the Flash-back machine (Fancy Pants Adventure, Alien Hominid), racers and runners (HexGL supports gamepad natively, check its controls line), and anything in the Player. Stick to keyboard and mouse for: idle games, puzzle games, text adventures like Zork, and the strategy shelf, a pad adds nothing there. When in doubt, the game's controls line tells you what's intended.

### Troubleshooting: the honest list

- Pad not detected: press any button after the page loads (browsers only list pads after first input), then check html5gamepad.com. Still nothing? Try USB.
- Wrong button does the thing: the game assumed the standard mapping and your pad is exotic. Remap it in the Player's per-system remapper, or check the tester's mapping.
- Two pads, wrong one is Player 1: browsers order pads by connection order, unplug and reconnect in the order you want them.
- Steam is running: Steam's controller layer can swallow inputs before the browser sees them. Quit Steam or disable its controller support for desktop.
- It works everywhere except one game: that game polls getGamepads() once at load instead of every frame. Reload the page with the pad already connected and press a button on the title screen.

## PICO-8 spotlight: the fantasy console's best corners
Difficulty: Beginner · ~15 min · slug: pico8-spotlight

Meet the fantasy console with thousands of tiny games: Splore, the Lexaloffle BBS, where the gems hide, and how to play everything free in your browser.

### What PICO-8 is

PICO-8 is a 'fantasy console' by Lexaloffle: a fake 1980s machine with deliberately tiny limits (128x128 pixels, 16 colors, 32KB cartridges) that runs on your real computer. The limits are the point, they force small, finished, weird games, and the community has made thousands of them. The software itself costs $15 and is worth it if you want to make games; playing other people's games in the browser is completely free.

### Splore: the built-in game browser

Inside PICO-8, type splore at the command prompt and hit enter. Splore is a graphical cartridge explorer: it browses games published to the community BBS over the internet, right from inside the console. Pick a cart, it downloads and runs. Press Esc to pause any cart and hop back to Splore. It's the closest thing retro gaming has to a streaming service, except everything is tiny and free.

### The BBS: where the carts live

The Lexaloffle BBS (lexaloffle.com/bbs) is the official community hub: every published cartridge gets a page where anyone can play it in the browser, no PICO-8 purchase needed, star it, favorite it, and download the .p8.png cartridge file. The BBS sorts by featured, new, and top-rated, and the comments are where developers explain their tricks. If Splore is the storefront, the BBS is the town square.

### Where the gems hide

Start with the BBS 'featured' and top-rated sorts, curation by thousands of players beats any algorithm. Then follow developers: PICO-8's best creators publish repeatedly, and their BBS profiles are discographies. Check the carts linked from this site's pico8-gems collection for a hand-picked starting shelf. And don't sleep on tweetcarts: 140-character games that fit in a post, some of them genuinely brilliant.

### Playing in your browser (free)

Every BBS cartridge page has a built-in web player, click and play, no install, no account. Developers can also export any cart as a standalone HTML5 page, which is why PICO-8 games show up embedded across the web. Keyboard controls are the default (arrows + Z/X); many web exports also accept gamepads. Your progress saves in the browser like any web game.

### The pico8-gems shelf

This site's pico8-gems collection is the curated on-ramp: a Doom demake, the original Celeste, and other standout carts, each linking to its official BBS page. Play the shelf first, then use the BBS sorts above to go deeper. If a shelf game hooks you, its BBS page links the developer's other carts, that's the rabbit hole, and it's a good one.

### Make your first cart (the 10-minute version)

If the $15 calls to you: PICO-8's editor is code, sprites, map, sound, and music in one window, all in Lua. The built-in help and the official manual walk you from a blank cart to a moving sprite in minutes. Publish to the BBS when it does something fun, the community plays and comments on everything, including gloriously broken first attempts. The legal lane is clean by design: every cart is its author's original work.

### Why it matters

PICO-8 proved that constraints make better games and friendlier developers. Thousands of people finished and shipped something, most for the first time in their lives, because the canvas was small enough to fill. Whether you play the shelf, browse the BBS, or buy the console and make your own, you're participating in the healthiest corner of game development. Start with someone else's cart. End with your own.

## Cheat codes, decoded: Game Genie, GameShark & the Konami Code
Difficulty: Beginner · ~12 min · slug: cheat-codes

Every cheat code is an address plus a value. Covers the two families (RAM codes vs ROM patches), the Konami Code's origin (Hashimoto, the 1986 NES Gradius port, Contra's 30 lives in 1988), the Game Genie (Codemasters/Galoob, 1990; six-letter codes patch unconditionally, eight-letter codes add a compare byte), the 1992 Ninth Circuit ruling in Lewis Galoob Toys v. Nintendo that made home cheat use fair use, GameShark/Action Replay (Datel hardware, InterAct's US brand from 1996), cheats in this site's Player (per-game codes via the Cheats tool, EJS_cheats, toggled in the in-game menu), finding your own codes with a RetroArch memory search, and where cheats don't belong (multiplayer, hardcore achievements). Legal lane: codes are numbers, never downloads.

### What a cheat code actually is

An address plus a value: somewhere in memory the game keeps a number (lives, health, ammo), and a code changes it or holds it. Two families: RAM codes (watch/poke working memory; GameShark, Action Replay, most emulator engines) and ROM patches (change what the program says as it is read; the Game Genie). Codes are written for one version of one game, region and revision are part of the code.

### Built-in codes: the Konami Code

Up Up Down Down Left Right Left Right B A. Written by Konami programmer Kazuhisa Hashimoto for the 1986 NES port of Gradius because he could not beat his own port while testing; it granted the full power-up set and shipped still in the game. Contra's NES release (1988) made it legend with 30 lives. Also: debug leftovers, password back doors, name-entry codes.

### The Game Genie: a cartridge that lies

Codemasters developed it; Galoob sold it in the US (Camerica in Canada); NES debut 1990. A pass-through cartridge between game and console that serves a different byte when a targeted ROM address is read, the cartridge itself is never modified. Six-letter codes decode to address + replacement, applied unconditionally; eight-letter codes add a compare byte so bank-switched games are only patched when the right bank is showing.

### The court case that made it legal

Nintendo sued Galoob, arguing derivative works; US sales were halted mid-case. The district court ruled for Galoob in 1991 and the Ninth Circuit affirmed in 1992 (Lewis Galoob Toys, Inc. v. Nintendo of America, Inc.): no permanent altered copy exists once the power is off, and home use is fair use. Sega instead gave the Genesis version its official seal of approval. The ruling is the ground emulator cheat engines stand on; it never licensed distributing games.

### GameShark & Action Replay: the RAM years

Datel's Action Replay went after RAM, where disc-era games keep health, money, and items. InterAct sold Datel's devices in the US from 1996 under the GameShark name, same hardware family, different badge, interchangeable codes. Codes are barely-encoded hex: address, value. Pro models added code searching, the skill section 7 teaches.

### Cheats in emulators & this site's Player

Emulator cores decode Genie/GameShark/Action Replay formats to address-and-value pairs, applied per core, support varies and nothing is guaranteed. In this site's Player: boot your game, add named codes under the Cheats card; they are stored per game in your browser, handed to the engine's cheat manager (EJS_cheats) before boot, and toggled from the cheat icon in the in-game menu.

### Find your own codes: the memory search

Any number a game displays lives at an address. RetroArch's built-in cheat search (since 1.7.4; Quick Menu -> Cheats -> Start or Continue Cheat Search) finds it by elimination: snapshot memory, change the number in-game, keep only addresses that moved the right way (less/greater/exact), repeat until a handful remain, then add and test them one at a time. Traps: transformed values (search direction, not exact) and display-copy decoy addresses.

### Cheat manners: where codes don't belong

Single-player: your game, your difficulty dial. Multiplayer/netplay: off-limits, tampering with a shared session, and one side's altered memory desyncs the rest. Hardcore achievement modes lock cheats out by design. Practice: keep one clean save no cheat session touches, and stack codes one at a time so the last added is the first suspect when something freezes.
